extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, advocates, DHS adjudicators, and stakeholders (e.g., attorneys, applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and interpretive guidance for making public charge inadmissibility determinations under INA section 212(a)(4), including which benefits and factors officers should consider and how they should be weighed in the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likely at any time to become a public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: The public charge inadmissibility determination is a forward-looking, prospective determination of a noncitizen's likelihood of becoming a public charge 'at any time' and is made at the time of the application for a visa, admission, or adjustment of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prospective standard follows the statutory phrase 'likely at any time' and DHS declines to limit the forward-looking window. The determination is necessarily subjective ('in the opinion of' DHS) and should be based on the totality of the circumstances at application time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'likely' (standard of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS continues to interpret 'likely' consistent with the 2019 Final Rule definition as 'more likely than not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS does not further define 'likely' beyond 'more likely than not' and declines to provide an additional regulatory definition; officers should apply a fact-specific discretionary determination consistent with that standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed temporal limit for the prospective test
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not limit the forward-looking aspect of the public charge determination to any specific period (for example, 3 or 5 years) because Congress used the phrase 'at any time' without temporal limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although fixed time limits might offer administrability, DHS declines them as not authorized by statute; officers must evaluate likelihood over an indefinite future horizon using available evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary dependence standard ('primarily dependent on the government for subsistence')
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is a public charge if they are primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, evidenced by receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'primarily dependent' standard identifies individuals dependent without other sufficient means. It does not require prolonged, exclusive, or permanent dependence, though persistent/exclusive dependence strongly supports inadmissibility. Short-term or supplementary benefit use (e.g., brief rehabilitation institutionalization) ordinarily will not constitute primary dependence. Positive factors (assets, income, sponsors) can overcome negative implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits considered: public cash assistance for income maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider public cash assistance for income maintenance (including SSI, TANF, and State, Tribal, territorial, or local cash benefit programs for income maintenance) when assessing likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of such cash benefits, even for a short period, may be probative; officers should consider recency, amount, and duration. DHS rejects limiting consideration to federal-only cash programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits considered: long-term institutionalization at government expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term institutionalization at government expense is a ground for finding primary dependence and therefore is a benefit category DHS will consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medicaid qualifies only when used for long-term institutionalization. Short-term institutionalization for rehabilitation would not constitute primary dependence. Evidence of long-term institutionalization indicates persistent dependence and weighs heavily in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of most non-cash benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider most non-cash, supplemental, or special-purpose benefit programs (e.g., SNAP, CHIP, WIC, school nutrition, home energy assistance, childcare assistance, most Medicaid benefits, HCBS) when making public charge determinations, with the narrow exception of Medicaid when used for long-term institutionalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programs are excluded because they often support employment and self-sufficiency and are not treated as indicators of primary dependence. Officers should not treat participation in these programs as evidence of being a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of disaster and pandemic assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Disaster or pandemic assistance (e.g., emergency benefits in response to hurricanes, wildfires, pandemics) will not be considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such assistance is for a specific purpose and should not be used as predictive evidence of future primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy-related and temporary benefits treated in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of benefits during pregnancy or for temporary circumstances is not categorically excluded, but DHS may take the surrounding circumstances into account in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will not broadly exclude all benefits received during pregnancy (or temporary supports) because in some cases recency, amount, and duration could be probative; officers should consider context and purpose of benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of recency, amount, and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: When past or current receipt of public cash assistance or long-term institutionalization is present, DHS will consider the recency, amount, and duration of such receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer-ago receipt generally carries less weight; greater duration or larger amounts of receipt strengthen the implication of future primary dependence. Officers must weigh these elements within the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past or current receipt may be probative but is not outcome-determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS considers past or current receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization as potentially probative of future primary dependence, but such evidence is part of a totality-of-circumstances analysis and can be overcome by positive factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress' treatment (e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1641(c) carve-outs) indicates past benefit receipt may be considered for some classes. Officers should not treat benefit receipt as dispositive without assessing mitigating evidence (assets, employment prospects, sponsors).

rubrics_metrics.name: No numerical thresholds or bright-line dollar/percent tests
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not adopt numerical thresholds (e.g., cash assistance composing 75% of income or dollar cutoffs) to define 'primarily dependent' or to determine public charge status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS considers 'primarily' in its ordinary meaning and finds numerical thresholds unnecessary and potentially arbitrary; individualized determinations are preferred over one-size-fits-all bright-lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refugees and asylees exempt from public charge consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Refugees and asylees are statutorily exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility and DHS will not consider any public benefits received by these populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exemption is codified in regulatory provisions (8 CFR 212.23(a)(1) and (2)); officers must not include benefits received by exempt groups in public charge analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability cannot be the sole basis for a public charge finding
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS cannot use the very fact of disability alone to conclude that a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While benefits used by individuals with disabilities (e.g., SSI) may be considered as part of the totality of circumstances, officers must not rely solely on disability status; they should evaluate related evidence (income, assets, supports) and may record financial circumstances neutrally when benefits represent the only income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household income calculation excludes certain public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The noncitizen's household income does not include income from public benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text clarifies that household income and past/current receipt of benefits are treated separately for the purposes of the forms and adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-485 collects household income separately from benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant changes to the Form I-485 collect information regarding the noncitizen's household income, assets, and financial status separately from information about past or current receipt of public benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural separation is intended to ensure officers evaluate financial resources and benefit use distinctly in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers should analyze statutorily enumerated factors in context and DHS will issue guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When making public charge determinations, officers are to analyze the factors set forth in the rule in the context of each noncitizen's individual circumstances; DHS plans to issue guidance to improve consistent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is intended to better ensure the regulatory standard is appropriately and consistently applied; however, such guidance will not be outcome determinative and decisions remain individualized and discretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: State, Tribal, territorial, and local cash assistance included
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider State, Tribal, territorial, and local cash assistance programs for income maintenance, not only Federal programs, when they are indicative of primary dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of non-federal cash assistance generally serves the same predictive purpose as federal cash assistance; officers should weigh recency, amount, and duration similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-dollar benefit receipt under prior rule not dispositive here
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS rejects the 2019 Final Rule's bright-line approach that could deem applicants public charges for receipt of small-dollar benefits (e.g., $20/month SNAP), finding such an approach overbroad and not consistent with historical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will not automatically penalize low-level, intermittent benefit receipt; officers should treat small or infrequent payments as limited evidence, evaluated in the broader totality analysis.
